approach: A two-stage LIVE screen, not a backtested strategy. Stage 1 is a hard-filter gate that removes anything violating the mandate or failing quality, applied to the ~2,100 companies where a balance sheet and a price both exist. Stage 2 ranks the survivors on a composite of cheapness-within-peer-group and quality, then a human applies sector caps to the top ~30 to land on 10 positions. Critically, the choice of valuation multiple is made from DEPRECIATION INTENSITY (depreciation/revenue, median split of the universe) rather than from a sector label, because 58% of our universe has no sector label at all. High depreciation intensity routes to EV/EBITDA, low routes to P/E. This gets the investor's sector-appropriate-multiple rule without depending on data we mostly do not have. I verified the funnel end to end: 2,098 names merge price to financials, 1,664 pass liquidity, 1,481 pass D/E<=1.5, 700 pass ROCE>12%, 696 are profitable, 414 remain after the no-recent-rally gate. That is a workable pool to rank down to 10, so the design is feasible on today's data in shape, though not in freshness (see data_we_lack #1).
thesis: The investor has three structural edges and this design tries to use only those, not to discover a new factor. First, Rs 50k per position lets him own genuinely small, thinly-covered companies where the price is set by retail flow rather than by analysts, which is where a mechanical value-and-quality filter has historically had the most room to work. Second, a 10-name concentrated book means the screen does not need to be right on average across hundreds of stocks; it needs to surface thirty defensible candidates from which a human picks ten, which is a far lower statistical bar than a factor portfolio. Third, no fixed horizon and no redemption pressure means he can hold through the multi-year re-rating that value requires, which is exactly the period over which leveraged and impatient holders are forced out. The quality overlay (ROCE above WACC, leverage cap, accrual check) exists solely to avoid the value trap, because we already know the median Indian stock LAGS the index and only 42.6% beat it, so buying cheap indiscriminately is buying the losing half of that distribution. The screen's whole claim is narrow: cheap AND demonstrably earning above its cost of capital AND not levered AND not already re-rated is a better-than-random starting pool for human judgement. It is not a claim of measured alpha, because as stated below we cannot measure it.
hard_filters: LIQUIDITY: median daily turnover over the trailing 12 months >= Rs 20 lakh. At Rs 50k a position this is ~2.5% of a day's volume, so impact cost stays negligible while still admitting genuinely small names. Removes 434 of 2,098.

LEVERAGE: debt_to_equity <= 1.5, from the most recent half-yearly balance sheet (debt_long + debt_short) / equity. Mandate constant, not tunable. Removes a further 183. NOTE: this rule mechanically excludes every bank and NBFC, whose D/E runs 6-10x by construction. The investor's P/B and P/Adjusted-BV branch for lenders is therefore MOOT in this screen. Financials need a separate screen with different fields, and our data (no NIM, no GNPA, no provisions, no tier-1) cannot support one today.

RETURN ON CAPITAL: ROCE = annualised EBIT / (equity + debt_total) > 12%, the top of his stated 10-12% WACC band. EBIT is derived as ebitda - depreciation, where ebitda already strips other_income (treasury yield is not the business earning anything). This is the single most destructive filter, cutting 1,481 to 700, which is the correct behaviour: most listed Indian companies do not clear their cost of capital.

PROFITABLE ON NORMALISED EARNINGS: profit_normalised > 0, i.e. after stripping exceptional_items. Only removes 4 more names but it is the filter that stops a one-off land sale from dressing up a loss-making business, which the investor explicitly asked for.
NOT ALREADY RE-RATED: last close <= 85% of the trailing 12-month high. This is the operational form of 'entry before a rally' and is discussed honestly in entry_rule. Cuts 696 to 414.

ACCRUAL / CASH-QUALITY CHECK: working capital intensity ((current_assets - current_liabilities) / revenue) must not have risen more than 25% between the two available balance-sheet dates. This is a WEAK SUBSTITUTE for cash conversion, not cash conversion itself, because we have no cash flow statement at all. Computable for 1,279 symbols; a company that fails to compute is flagged for manual reading, not silently passed.

MANUAL, NOT CODED: promoter pledging low or clearly justified. This cannot be enforced in code (see data_we_lack #5). It is a per-finalist manual check on the NSE encumbrance filing before any capital is committed, and it is a veto.
ranking_factors: CHEAPNESS WITHIN DEPRECIATION-INTENSITY BUCKET (weight 40%): percentile rank of the appropriate multiple against peers in the same bucket. High-depreciation bucket (capital-intensive: telecom, infra, steel, cement, hotels, hospitals, power) ranks on EV/EBITDA, where EV = price*shares_implied + debt_total. Low-depreciation bucket (asset-light: IT services, mature consumer, services) ranks on P/E on annualised profit_normalised. Percentile rank rather than an absolute threshold is deliberate, because the absolute numbers carry a known ~15% market-cap error.
QUALITY, i.e. ROCE percentile within the same bucket (weight 30%). Ranking ROCE rather than merely gating on it is what tilts the final ten toward the better businesses inside the cheap pool.

MARGIN STABILITY (weight 15%): standard deviation of EBITDA margin across the 1-3 available quarters, inverted. This is a deliberately low weight because with at most three observations it is a very noisy estimate; it is included to penalise obvious volatility, not to measure it precisely.

BALANCE SHEET HEADROOM (weight 15%): D/E percentile within bucket, inverted, so that among two equally cheap and equally profitable names the less levered one wins. This deliberately double-counts leverage (it is already a hard filter) because leverage is the mechanism by which a value position becomes an unrecoverable loss rather than a long wait.

TIE-BREAK, NOT SCORED: current_assets/current_liabilities > 1 and the accrual check comfortably passed. Used to separate near-identical composite scores rather than as a weighted term, since adding a fifth weight adds an overfitting surface for very little discrimination.
entry_rule: Buy when a name is in the top 30 of the composite ranking AND passes every hard filter AND the manual pledge/promoter check. Enter in two tranches of Rs 25k, the second only after 60 calendar days, and place the second tranche regardless of whether the position is up or down, so that averaging in is a rule rather than a decision made in the moment. There is NO price-momentum confirmation and no requirement that the stock has stopped falling, because any such confirmation is momentum by another name and he has explicitly rejected it. I want to be honest about the wording here, because it matters: 'entry before a rally' is not an observable condition at entry time. Nobody can filter on a rally that has not happened. What is actually implementable is 'entry without a preceding rally', which is what the <=85%-of-12-month-high gate does, and those are different things. The gate guarantees he is not buying after a run; it guarantees nothing about a run following. The direct and accepted cost is that he will frequently be early, and sometimes the stock is cheap and below its high because the business is genuinely deteriorating in ways our three quarters of data cannot see. The staged entry and the stop below are what make being early survivable rather than a design flaw.
exit_rules: WRITTEN AT ENTRY, ONE PAGE PER POSITION: the specific multiple paid, the ROCE at purchase, the D/E at purchase, and the one sentence saying what would have to become false for the thesis to be dead. No position is opened without this page. Every rule below is checked against that page, not against how the position feels.

VALUATION EXIT: sell when the entry multiple has re-rated to the bucket MEDIAN. This is the exit for a position that WORKED, and it exists specifically because his stated failure mode is holding winners past the point of thesis completion. When it triggers, it is not a judgement call.
LEVERAGE BREAK: sell at the next half-yearly balance sheet if D/E exceeds 1.5. Non-negotiable, mandate-level, no grace period.
QUALITY BREAK: sell if ROCE falls below 12% for two consecutive readings. Two readings rather than one because a single annualised quarter is a noisy estimate and would otherwise churn the book.

HARD STOP: -25% from average cost, on a weekly closing basis rather than intraday so that a single bad print does not eject a sound position. Weekly-close is chosen because it cannot be gamed in the moment; he checks it once a week or not at all.

TIME STOP: 18 months from first tranche with no thesis progress, where progress is defined ONLY as revenue growth or ROCE improvement versus the entry page. A cheap stock that stays cheap for 18 months while the business does not improve is capital that is doing nothing, and this rule is what stops the long-term sleeve becoming a place where mistakes go to be forgotten.
RE-ENTRY LOCKOUT: no re-entry into a stopped-out name for 90 days. This is aimed squarely at the panic-sell-then-revenge-buy loop he described.

SECTOR CAP ENFORCED AT EXIT TOO: if a sector reaches 4 names through anything other than the pre-agreed urgent exception, the lowest-composite-ranked name in that sector is sold, chosen by the ranking and not by which one he likes least.
data_we_lack: STALENESS, AND IT IS DISQUALIFYING TODAY: financials stop at the September 2025 quarter, last broadcast 2025-11-06. Prices run to 2026-09-07. The December 2025, March 2026 and June 2026 quarters are entirely absent, so the screen is ~10 months blind. This is a DESIGN, not a signal that can be acted on this week. The financials backfill must catch up before a single rupee moves, and the exit rules keyed to half-yearly balance sheets are equally inert until then.

NO TRAILING TWELVE MONTHS, FOR ANYONE. Only three period_ends exist (2025-03, 2025-06, 2025-09) and TTM needs four. Worse, only 620 of 2,216 symbols have all three; 1,041 have two and 555 have just one. Earnings must be annualised from 1-3 quarters, which will badly misprice every seasonal or cyclical business (sugar, cement, travel, agrochemicals) and will do so in the most dangerous direction: a cyclical at peak quarterly earnings screens as cheap on P/E precisely at the top.

NO CASH FLOW STATEMENT AT ALL. There is no CFO, no capex, no free cash flow, no CFO/EBITDA. The brief explicitly asked for 'real cash conversion' and I cannot deliver it. The working-capital accrual check I substituted uses two balance-sheet dates six months apart and is a much blunter instrument that will miss receivables-financed fake revenue in any company whose game is slower than one half-year.

NO SHARES OUTSTANDING. shares_implied is back-solved as profit/EPS and it is unstable: Reliance computes 15.64bn, 15.38bn, 16.50bn across three consecutive quarters, a ~7% swing, and sits roughly 15% above the true post-bonus count. Every market-cap-derived number (P/E, EV/EBITDA, P/B) inherits this. My live check put Reliance at Rs 20.5 lakh crore against a real ~Rs 17-18 lakh crore. This is why ranking_factors uses percentile ranks, not absolute cut-offs, but percentiles do not repair the error, they only stop it being the whole decision.

NO PROMOTER PLEDGE PERCENTAGE, so one of his two stated HARD LIMITS is not enforceable in code. The 'pledge' category holds 4,187 filings but they are dominated by promoter-reclassification notices, and only 34 rows in the entire 706,128-row announcements table contain any percentage figure at all. The yearly counts (3,375 in 2022, then 198, 253, 261, 100) describe the categoriser's behaviour, not corporate India's. The actual numbers live inside linked PDFs we do not parse.

NO SECTOR CLASSIFICATION for most of the universe. Only 923 of the 2,216 companies with financials carry any industry label, it comes from announcement metadata rather than a real taxonomy, and its 75 buckets are inconsistent ('Textiles - Cotton' vs 'Textile Products' vs 'Textiles - Synthetic'). The max-3-per-sector rule cannot be automated across the universe.

NO SHAREHOLDING PATTERN of any kind: no promoter holding %, no pledge, no FII/DII, no changes over time. Also no auditor resignations, no related-party transactions, no contingent liabilities, no order book, no segment reporting. Several of these are the classic small-cap fraud tells, and this screen is aimed squarely at small caps.

NO HISTORY, THEREFORE NO BACKTEST AND NO TUNING. Three half-yearly balance sheets cannot establish whether low leverage, high ROCE or cheapness predicted anything. No event study, no trial count, no deflated Sharpe is available for the fundamental side of this design. Every fundamental threshold below is set from economic reasoning and frozen, and I want to be explicit that this means they are UNVALIDATED, not that they are safe.
SPARSE BALANCE SHEET EVEN WHERE IT EXISTS: equity fills 48.6% of rows, borrowings 44.6%, current assets 45.4%. Some companies omit the tags even in March and September filings.

CONSOLIDATED/STANDALONE MIXING: only 470 symbols have three consolidated quarters. Falling back to standalone for the rest (which my dry run did, to reach usable coverage) makes cross-sectional multiples quietly inconsistent, since standalone hides subsidiary debt and subsidiary earnings both.

NO GOODWILL OR INTANGIBLES BREAKOUT, so capital employed cannot be adjusted for acquisitions and ROCE is flattered for serial acquirers, which is precisely the profile that most often blows up in Indian small caps.

SURVIVORSHIP RETURNS THROUGH THE BACK DOOR: prices are survivorship-free, but financials only cover companies currently filing. The screen's universe is therefore survivorship-biased even though the price archive is not, and any future attempt to test this screen historically would inherit that bias.
sector_handling: Two mechanisms, because sector is doing two different jobs and only one of them can be automated. JOB ONE, choosing the multiple: handled WITHOUT sector labels, by splitting the universe at its median depreciation/revenue ratio. Above the median the business is capital-intensive and depreciation distorts earnings, so it ranks on EV/EBITDA; below it, on P/E. This reproduces the intent of his rule (EV/EBITDA for telecom, infra, steel, cement, hotels, hospitals; P/E for IT services and mature consumer) from a field that is 96.4% populated, instead of from a label that is missing for 58% of the universe. It will occasionally misclassify an asset-heavy consumer company, which is an acceptable error and a visible one. JOB TWO, the max-3-per-sector concentration cap: NOT automated. The announcement-derived industry label covers 923 of 2,216 companies in 75 inconsistent buckets and is not trustworthy enough to enforce a risk limit. Instead the cap is applied by hand to the top ~30 ranked candidates, which is entirely tractable at this portfolio size and is the correct division of labour: a ten-name book only ever needs thirty sector assignments. Where a label exists it is shown as a prompt, and correlation of the stock to the seventeen Nifty sector indices we hold daily since 2015 is offered as an automated cross-check on any assignment that looks wrong. Banks and NBFCs never reach this stage because the D/E<=1.5 mandate filter removes them mechanically.
how_it_could_fail: The most likely failure is the ordinary one: this is a value screen in a market where only 42.6% of stocks beat the index and the median stock lags, so 'cheap and below its high' is a description of the losing half of the distribution, and the quality overlay may simply not be a strong enough filter to fix that. The second failure is specific and sharp: annualising one to three quarters means a cyclical at peak earnings shows a low P/E and a high ROCE at exactly the moment it is most dangerous, so this screen is structurally biased toward buying cyclical tops, and the ROCE filter makes that worse rather than better because peak-cycle ROCE is peak too. Third, the ~15% market-cap error from EPS-implied share counts is not random noise; it is largest for companies with recent bonuses, splits or convertibles, so the ranking is systematically distorted toward a particular kind of company. Fourth, the 10-month data gap means that even once the backfill lands, the screen at any moment is reading a business that has since had two or three unobserved quarters, and small-cap theses change faster than that. Fifth, the no-recent-rally gate cannot distinguish 'cheap and unloved' from 'falling for a reason we cannot see', and with no cash flow statement, no shareholding data and no pledge numbers, the reasons we cannot see include most of the ones that actually matter. Finally, the honest structural point: 414 names survive the filters and ten are chosen from a ranking built on measurement error of this size, so the gap between this screen and picking ten reasonable-looking companies by hand may be smaller than the apparatus suggests. The apparatus's defensible contribution is not the ranking, it is the pre-committed exits, which address the failure mode he actually named.
